# Block 8: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged {.unnumbered} You have a computation that already works and you want to tidy it into a reusable function. An agent can do that in seconds; doing it yourself takes a little longer. Either way the hard part is not the refactor, it is the verification: a change that "improves" code can quietly alter its output, so how do you confirm the function still does what the script did? The method this block teaches is to freeze the original result before anything is touched. You run the analysis once, save its output to a reference file (an `.rds`), and then require the new function to reproduce that reference exactly. This is a *characterisation test*: it does not assert the answer is correct, only that it is *unchanged*. That distinction is the whole point, and Step 4 returns to it. The block has a shared spine and then three paths that differ only in who writes the function and the test: - **Path A — by hand.** You write the function and the test yourself. Slowest, and the one that teaches the verification logic most directly. Start here if testthat is new. - **Path B — delegate in two steps.** You instruct an in-IDE agent to do the refactor and the test, in two separate prompts, and you verify between them. - **Path C — encode it as a skill.** Conceptual only. You see how the trust rule, once understood, can be bundled into a reusable instruction for an agent, and why that is a sharper knife than it first appears. Paths A and B are the substance. Path C only makes sense once you have done one of them, because a skill hides the very boundary the earlier paths make you type out. *⏱ ~45 minutes* ## The repository layout ``` repo/ ├── .github/ │ └── workflows/ │ ├── r-checks.yml the independent check (runs on GitHub) │ └── copilot-setup-steps.yml the cloud agent's environment ├── data/ │ └── voles_metabolism.csv the dataset (contains one NA, on purpose) ├── scripts/ │ ├── 01_load_data.R loads the CSV, runs glimpse() │ ├── 02_analysis.R the original script; later calls the function │ └── functions/ │ └── summary_functions.R the extracted function (you or the agent) ├── tests/ │ ├── make_reference.R captures the reference │ └── metabolic_summary.rds you generate this in Step 0, then freeze it │ └── test_summary_functions.R compares the function against the reference └── renv.lock pins tidyverse, here, testthat, renv ``` The single most important property of this layout: the `.rds` under `tests/` is generated by you and by nobody else. Everything else in the trust argument follows from that, and it holds identically across all three paths. ## The original script `R/01_load_data.R` reads the CSV into `voles` and runs `glimpse()`. Its `col_types` specification is shown in full because the reference and the test must read the data identically; an unspecified type here is the silent mismatch the environment section warns about. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/01_load_data.R library(tidyverse) library(here) voles <- readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "voles_metabolism.csv"), col_types = readr::cols( treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double() ) ) glimpse(voles) ``` ::: `R/02_analysis.R` sources it and computes the summary you will functionalise: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/02_analysis.R — the original, trusted version library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here::here("scripts", "01_load_data.R")) metabolic_summary <- voles |> group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |> summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = n(), .groups = "drop" ) ``` ::: Two things to note now and leave alone. First, the dataset contains one missing value in `metabolic_rate_post` and this computation has no `na.rm`, so one cell of the result will be `NA`. That is deliberate and it matters in Step 4; do not "fix" it yet. Second, `group_by()` sorts its grouping keys in the output, whereas the `.by` argument introduced in Path A does not. The supplied `voles_metabolism.csv` is ordered so that the first appearance of the grouping keys does not match their sorted order, which means the unpatched `.by` function produces a genuinely different row arrangement. That fact returns in Step 2. ## Step 0 (spine) — You capture the reference Before anything else, run `R/02_analysis.R` yourself and confirm `metabolic_summary` looks as you expect, including the one `NA` cell, which is expected. Then run the capture script below once and keep the resulting `.rds`. This frozen output is the trust anchor. Capture it now, before any refactor: afterwards `02_analysis.R` computes the summary through the very function under test, so re-capturing would compare the function against itself. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/fixtures/make_reference.R # Run this BEFORE refactoring, and capture only once. source(here::here("scripts", "02_analysis.R")) saveRDS( metabolic_summary, here::here("tests", "metabolic_summary.rds") ) ``` ::: You now hold the reference. The three paths differ only in who produces the function and the test that must reproduce it. Pick one path, then rejoin at the environment section and Step 4. ## Path A — Write the function and test yourself Write the function in `functions/summary_functions.R`. A first attempt that a tidy refactor naturally reaches for uses the modern `.by` argument:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R — first attempt, deliberately incomplete summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) } ``` :::
Above is a test example that will trigger a deliberate issue! Write the test of the function above and run it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_summary_functions.R library(testthat) source(here::here("functions", "summary_functions.R")) test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate reproduces the original summary", { reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")) voles <- readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "voles_metabolism.csv"), col_types = readr::cols( treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double() ) ) expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(voles), reference, tolerance = 1e-8) }) ``` :::
Run it with `testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R"))`. It fails, and not on the numbers. Because the supplied dataset is ordered so that first appearance differs from sorted order (noted above), `.by` returns the rows in a different arrangement from the `group_by()` that produced your reference. The values are right; the rows are arranged differently, and `expect_equal()` reports a mismatch. Add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` to the end of the pipeline and it passes. That failure is the lesson in miniature: a change that improves the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it.
While you are writing the test by hand, resist one specific temptation. Do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals. If you hard-code the values you saw, the test no longer compares against your frozen reference; it compares the function against numbers you transcribed, which proves nothing about whether the refactor preserved the original computation. The test must *read the `.rds`*. That is the one non-negotiable line, and writing it yourself is how you learn why. The `col_types` specification is deliberate, and it matches the one in `scripts/01_load_data.R` exactly. Letting `read_csv` guess types can produce a column type that differs from the one stored in the reference, causing a mismatch that has nothing to do with the refactor. Column types are the finest-grained version of a broader concern, the environment the test runs in, which the environment section below addresses. When a characterisation test fails, suspect this kind of difference before suspecting the code. The function you should converge on, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # R/functions/summary_functions.R — final #' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex #' #' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and #' metabolic_rate_post. #' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, giving the mean, #' standard deviation and n. summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } dplyr::group_by(data, treatment_arm, sex) |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop" ) } ``` :::
Finally, edit `R/02_analysis.R` to call `summarise_metabolic_rate()` instead of the inline pipeline, so the function genuinely replaces the code it came from. Rejoin at the environment section. ## Path B — Delegate the two steps to an agent Use this path if you want the agent to do the work while you verify. The key discipline is to split it into two prompts, not one. A single prompt that emits both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) propagate into both files at once, producing a green result that proves nothing. Separating the prompts keeps the verifier from inheriting the refactor's assumptions, which is the testing equivalent of keeping the `.rds` out of the agent's hands. **Prompt 1 — the refactor only:** ```text Move the computation in scripts/02_analysis.R into a documented function in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Have 02_analysis.R call the new function instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests yet, and do not touch anything under tests/. ``` Watch the agent edit the files in your editor and read what it writes to `R/functions/` as it appears. If it uses `.by` without a trailing `arrange()`, leave that for now; the next step will expose it. **Prompt 2 — the test only:** ```text Add tests/test_summary_functions.R that loads the reference tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, runs summarise_metabolic_rate(), and compares with expect_equal(). Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/. I captured that reference myself; a reference you generate proves nothing. ``` That last paragraph is the entire trust argument in three sentences. Before you trust the green tick, apply this checklist to whatever the agent wrote, reading the lines yourself: 1. The test *reads* `tests/metabolic_summary.rds` and compares against it. It does not hard-code expected numbers inside the test. If it does, the verification is circular whatever colour the result is. 2. The test calls `summarise_metabolic_rate()`, the actual function under test, not a reimplementation of the pipeline inside the test body. 3. Nothing under `tests/` was created or changed by the agent. Now run the test with `testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R"))`. If the agent's function used `.by` without `arrange()`, it fails on row order, not values, for the reason given in the spine. Have the agent add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` and run again. If it passed first time, force the failure yourself by removing the `arrange()`, so you see the mechanism rather than taking it on trust. Rejoin at the environment section. ## Path C — Encode the workflow as a skill (concept) This path is conceptual; you will not build a runnable file here. Notice that the trust paragraph you typed in Path B is a *durable convention*: it says the same thing every time, regardless of the analysis. Anything you find yourself retyping into every prompt is a candidate for a skill, a short standing instruction an agent loads and follows without being told afresh. A skill for this workflow would say, in essence: when asked to functionalise a script, capture the reference only if the human has not provided one, never regenerate a fixture under `tests/fixtures/`, refactor and test in separate steps, and compare against the human-held reference with `expect_equal()`. The benefit is obvious: you stop retyping the boundary. The hazard is exactly the same sentence read the other way. Once the rule lives in a skill, you no longer type it, no longer see it, and a colleague using your skill may never know the entire trust argument rests on a single line forbidding the agent from generating its own reference. The boundary becomes invisible, and an invisible boundary is precisely what Step 4 warns against in the statistical domain. A skill is therefore safe to use only once you have internalised what Paths A and B make explicit; it is a compression of that understanding, not a substitute for it. If you build one later, keep the "reference-stays-with-the-human" clause as a visible, commented line, so the boundary remains legible to whoever reads the skill next. ## The environment the test runs in (spine) A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The `col_types` specification in Path A handles the finest-grained version of that, a single column read; the rest of the environment, the R version and the entire package set, is handled by the two GitHub Actions workflows the template ships. Read them; do not write them. Recall from the GitHub session that GitHub Actions runs automated workflows in response to repository events such as a push or a pull request. Two such workflows sit in `.github/workflows/`, both placed there for you. `r-checks.yml` is the independent check. It runs the tests on pushes to `main` and on every pull request, from a clean checkout on GitHub's infrastructure. It is the check that neither you nor the agent can fake, and a green tick here is the signal you wait for at the end. `copilot-setup-steps.yml` is the cloud agent's environment. The cloud agent runs the tests in the environment this file builds, and if that environment does not restore `renv.lock`, the agent's tests will fail (or, worse, pass) for reasons that have nothing to do with the refactor, and the resemblance to your local setup is lost. Two requirements are load-bearing, and they fail in importantly different ways: - The job must be named exactly `copilot-setup-steps`. GitHub looks for that job name specifically; rename it and the agent silently falls back to a bare environment without your packages. - The job must restore the lockfile, so the agent computes against the same pinned package versions that `r-checks` will later use. Note the asymmetry between the two failure modes, because it determines which one you must watch for. A misnamed job fails loudly and safely: the fallback environment lacks your packages, so the tests typically error on the first missing function and you notice at once. A lockfile that restores subtly wrong versions fails quietly and dangerously: the tests run green against different package behaviour and certify invariance against the wrong baseline, which is exactly the failure the held `.rds` was meant to rule out. The self-announcing error is the lesser hazard; the silent green is the one that defeats your trust anchor. A conventional form, using the `r-lib/actions` setup actions, looks like the following. Check this against your actual template file rather than copying it blindly; this reproduces the standard pattern, not necessarily your exact configuration. :::{.callout-warning} This setup steers towards reproducibility because `setup-renv` reads `renv.lock` and installs the exact pinned versions, so the agent computes against the same package versions that `r-checks.yml` will later use from a clean checkout. This is what makes the agent's environment resemble your local IDE and is why the agent's test run and the independent check should agree. It is also what might make this workflow more fragile if the lockfile is out of step or does not restore packages. ::: ```yaml name: Copilot setup steps on: workflow_dispatch jobs: copilot-setup-steps: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: "4.5.2" # match the version in renv.lock use-public-rspm: true - name: Set up renv uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 env: RENV_CONFIG_PAK_ENABLED: "true" - name: Install Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 ``` `setup-renv` reads `renv.lock` and installs exactly the pinned versions, so the agent's tidyverse, here and testthat match yours. The final `Install Quarto` step is inherited from the wider template that renders the book; this chapter's tests are plain R and do not require it, so do not be surprised that nothing here uses it. The practical consequence: when you reach Step 4, the agent's own test run and the independent `r-checks` run should agree. If they disagree, suspect the environment before suspecting the code.
